answerKey.primaryProblem: Contact-lens-related microbial keratitis (corneal ulcer/infiltrate), right eye, until proven otherwise - risk factors include extended/overnight lens wear, water exposure (swimming/tap water rinse), and poor lens case hygiene. Pseudomonas and Acanthamoeba must be considered given water exposure.
differential: Bacterial microbial keratitis (including Pseudomonas, given lake/tap water exposure)
Acanthamoeba keratitis (given water exposure while wearing lenses)
Contact lens-related sterile corneal infiltrate (less likely given severity of pain, acuity loss, and photophobia)
Fungal keratitis (lower likelihood but relevant given water exposure)
keyFindings: Acute painful red right eye with marked photophobia and watery discharge, onset yesterday
Focal corneal white opacity/infiltrate visible on photo with surrounding haze
Visual acuity right eye reduced to counts-fingers from a baseline of 20/20
History of extended monthly lens wear stretched to ~2 months, overnight sleeping in lenses several nights per week
Lens worn while swimming in a lake and rinsed with tap water afterward
Patient reinserted contact lens this morning despite symptoms, to see for work
Patient used a friend's leftover steroid-antibiotic combination eye drop without professional guidance
Contact lens case shown on camera has cloudy/discolored solution, overdue for replacement, inconsistent with hygiene counseling given 14 months ago
plan: Instruct patient to remove and discontinue contact lens wear in right eye (and left eye) immediately
Advise against use of the borrowed steroid-antibiotic drop; discontinue immediately given risk of worsening infection/masking pseudomonas or fungal/Acanthamoeba keratitis with steroid component

Arrange same-day urgent referral to ophthalmology (cornea specialist or on-call ED ophthalmology) for corneal culture/scraping and smear, given sight-threatening presentation; corneal scraping and initiation of fortified topical antibiotics are outside optometry's scope and must be performed by ophthalmology - the optometrist's role is to recognize the emergency, stop harmful self-treatment, and ensure urgent hand-off
Instruct patient to bring current contact lenses and lens case/solution to the in-person visit for culture
Do not patch the eye; do not delay referral for home remedies

Counsel patient that this is outside safe scope for telehealth management alone and outside optometric scope for definitive treatment - visual acuity loss and corneal infiltrate require urgent in-person ophthalmologic slit lamp assessment and likely culture-directed fortified topical antibiotics
Document and report risk factors (extended wear, overnight wear, water exposure, non-prescribed steroid drop) for the receiving ophthalmology clinician
Arrange follow-up communication/contact with the in-person ophthalmology clinician or ED to confirm the patient was seen
redFlags: Marked reduction in visual acuity (counts fingers) in the affected eye
Corneal infiltrate/white spot visible on external photo
Severe photophobia and pain disproportionate to simple conjunctivitis
History of water exposure while wearing contact lenses (Acanthamoeba and Pseudomonas risk)
Use of a non-prescribed steroid-containing eye drop in the setting of a possible infectious corneal process
Overnight/extended contact lens wear as an ongoing risk behavior
educationPoints: Contact lens wearers with a painful red eye and vision change must be treated as having presumed microbial keratitis until an in-person slit lamp exam and culture rule it out

Overnight wear, extended replacement beyond manufacturer schedule, and water exposure (swimming, tap water rinsing) are major modifiable risk factors for contact-lens-related keratitis including Pseudomonas and Acanthamoeba

Topical steroids should never be used for a red eye of unclear or infectious cause without ophthalmic evaluation, as they can worsen bacterial, fungal, and Acanthamoeba keratitis and promote corneal melting

A corneal infiltrate with vision loss and significant pain is outside the scope of telehealth-only management and outside optometric scope for definitive treatment (corneal scraping, fortified antibiotics); it requires urgent referral to ophthalmology for in-person care and possible corneal scraping for microbiology
Patients may minimize or normalize risky lens hygiene behaviors ('I take care of them normally') and may need direct, nonjudgmental questioning to reveal the full history
Lens cases should be replaced regularly (e.g., every 1-3 months) and not allowed to accumulate cloudy or discolored solution, as biofilm formation increases infection risk

Optometrists play a critical triage role in recognizing sight-threatening presentations and must know the limits of their scope, ensuring timely referral to ophthalmology rather than attempting procedures like corneal scraping themselves

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient initially states he takes care of his contact lenses 'pretty normally, nothing weird'
mismatches.recordEvidence: Prior optometry note from 14 months ago documents he was specifically counseled on nightly removal, avoiding water exposure, and replacing lens case every 3 months - counseling that, per his own later admissions, he has not followed (stretching wear to 2 months, sleeping in lenses, swimming in lenses, not replacing case)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may underreport risky health behaviors when first asked in general terms; direct, specific, nonjudgmental questioning (and reviewing prior counseling documentation) is often needed to uncover true risk factors like extended wear, overnight wear, and water exposure.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient asks the learner to just prescribe something so he can keep wearing his lenses and get through the work week
mismatches.recordEvidence: Medication list and exam findings (visual acuity loss, corneal infiltrate on photo, no ocular medications on file) show this is a sight-threatening presentation requiring lens removal and same-day in-person referral, not a quick prescription to continue lens wear
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patient priorities and expectations (returning to normal activity quickly) can conflict with clinically necessary action; the learner must clearly explain why continuing lens wear or giving a quick-fix prescription is unsafe here and advocate for urgent in-person care despite the patient's work pressure.

objectives.text: Elicit a complete contact lens history including replacement schedule, overnight wear, and water exposure despite initial minimization by the patient, using direct interview questions beyond the patient's initial general reassurance
Recognize red flag signs of microbial keratitis (acute vision loss, corneal infiltrate, photophobia, pain) in a contact lens wearer via remote visual acuity testing and photo review
Identify unsafe self-treatment behaviors (reinserting lens, using borrowed steroid-antibiotic drops) and counsel the patient to stop them immediately
Formulate an appropriate triage and referral plan recognizing this presentation is outside safe scope for telehealth-only management, arranging same-day in-person evaluation with corneal scraping
Address patient goals and work pressure with empathetic communication while firmly explaining why continuing lens wear or a quick prescription is not appropriate
Differentiate relevant risk factors from distractors such as dry indoor air and seasonal allergy symptoms

scenario.studentBrief: You are an optometry student conducting a telehealth video visit. The patient, Kyle Andersen, a 25-year-old contact lens wearer, is calling about a painful red right eye that started yesterday. Take a focused ocular history, use remote exam techniques (camera inspection, patient-submitted photo, home visual acuity check) to assess severity, and determine the appropriate triage and management plan within your scope of practice.

tasks: Take a thorough history of the eye complaint including onset, pain, discharge, and vision changes
Take a detailed contact lens wear and hygiene history
Perform feasible remote exam elements: camera inspection, request a close-up photo, check visual acuity at home, and assess light sensitivity
Assess the severity of the presentation and determine the appropriate level and urgency of care
Communicate your management plan to the patient, including advice on contact lens wear and next steps

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in his apartment in Minneapolis, Minnesota
profile.summary: A 25-year-old contact lens wearer presents via telehealth with an acutely painful, photophobic, red right eye and vision loss after a weekend of swimming in lenses, extended lens wear, and overnight wear, compounded by self-treatment with a borrowed steroid-antibiotic drop. The case teaches optometry students to recognize contact-lens-related microbial keratitis as a sight-threatening emergency requiring immediate lens discontinuation, cessation of inappropriate steroid use, and same-day in-person referral for corneal scraping, rather than telehealth-only management.
